newsitem.title: USA: DOLE'S PROBLEM: even Republicans critical of him.
newsitem.headline: DOLE'S PROBLEM: even Republicans critical of him.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
One of Bob Dole's biggest problems is among Republicans.
With polls showing that only two of every three Republicans plan to vote for him, Dole is generating little enthusiasm even among some die-hard party members.

The 73-year-old Kansan's failure to solidify his base is a key reason why he trails President Bill Clinton by a double-digit margin in many polls, with less than six weeks to go until Election Day on Nov. 5.
In a Reuters poll of voters in Pennsylvania and New Jersey this week, Dole captured the support of only 62 percent of Republicans in Pennsylvania and 64 percent in New Jersey.
It was the same story in a Reuters poll of Illinois, Michigan and Ohio taken last week. Dole captured 66 percent of Republican votes in those crucial states.
Clinton, in contrast, is capturing 75-80 percent of his Democratic base as well as a majority of independents and a small but critical segment of Republican voters.

In two dozen follow-up interviews with voters, the magnitude of Dole's problem became clear. Voters worry about his age, see him as a political insider and criticise his lack of charisma on the campaign trail.

"I feel he's too much of an inside politician," said Mary Espinosa, a teacher's aide for handicapped children in Rahway, New Jersey, who voted for then-President George Bush in 1992 and for Republican Gov. Christine Todd Whitman in 1993 but is supporting Clinton this year.

"That slip up with cigarettes wasn't too smart. It showed me he's sold out teenagers because he's getting money from the tobacco industry," she said, referring to Dole's remarks several weeks ago that tobacco was not necessarily addictive.
Doris Clark, a retiree from Newcastle, Pennsylvania, supported Republican Gov. Tom Ridge in the state election only two years ago but says she will vote for Clinton in November.
"Nothing Dole could do or say will change my mind. He's an old politician. He only knows what's in Washington and he's been there too long," Clark said.
Several voters said they were voting for Dole primarily because of his selection of Jack Kemp as his vice presidential running mate.
"I'm supporting Jack Kemp. I'm not real impressed with Dole but when he picked Kemp as his running mate, I saw something solid," said Dennis Barger, a church pastor in Manahawkin, New Jersey.
"It's hard to put a finger on Dole's problems, but he's been in the Senate forever. He's a career politician and there's not a lot of pizzazz there," he said.

Wanda Gerhart, a machine operator from Gilbertsville, Pennsylvania, gave Dole a half-hearted endorsement. "When Dole picked Kemp, I felt a lot better. If Dole drops, we've got a better man behind him," Gerhart said.
Several voters were turned off by Dole's opposition to Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's participation in the upcoming presidential debates.

"I believe Perot should be allowed in, even though he's probably a threat to Dole. It (his exclusion) makes me less likely to vote for Dole," said Michael Horbacewicz, a computer engineer from Tenafly New Jersey.
Horbacewicz, who voted for Whitman for governor, said he was unimpressed with both Clinton and Dole and would vote for "the lesser of two evils."

This is precisely the kind of vote Dole must win to have any chance. But Horbacewicz's opinion of the Republican nominee was scathing. "He seems to believe he deserves the spot because he's been there so long," he said.
Some voters said Dole was spending too much time attacking Clinton and not enough telling the country in sufficient detail what he would as president.
"Dole has to talk more about what he's going to do and less about what Clinton said," said Nancy Geler, a Dole supporter from Pittsburgh.
Dole's 15 percent income tax-cut plan meets with widespread scepticism, even from Republicans.

"I don't agree with Dole's tax cut. Somewhere down the road, we'll all have to pay for it," said Gary Clemons, a casket maker in Mount Wolf, Pennsylvania, who nevertheless said he would support the Republican nominee.
